Naaman
nā'ă-măn
n. (Syrian captain, leper, and convert — the Gentile healed in Jordan whom the Lord Jesus named to a synagogue that tried to kill Him for it)
From Hebrew Na'aman, “pleasantness”, from na'em, to be pleasant or agreeable — the same root as Naomi. It is a name of grace on a man who had to be brought very low to receive any.

Biblical Definition

Naaman is introduced with a string of honours and one word that undoes them all: “captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper” (2Ki 5:1). Note who is said to have given Syria its victories. The gospel reaches him by the lowest possible channel — a captive Israelite girl waiting on his wife — and it reaches him crooked, through a king's letter and a diplomatic incident, before Elisha sends a messenger to the door with an order and does not come out himself. Naaman was furious: he had a script in his head about how a prophet should behave, and he had better rivers at home. His servants reasoned with him, and he went down. “Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean” (2Ki 5:14). What follows is a confession: “Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel” (2Ki 5:15). He asked for two mules' burden of earth to build an altar on, and asked pardon for the bowing he would still have to do in the house of Rimmon. The Lord Jesus cited him at Nazareth: “none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian” (Luk 4:27).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Naaman; in sacred history he is the captain of the host of the king of Syria, cleansed of leprosy by washing seven times in Jordan.

expand to see more

NAAMAN, n. Captain of the host of Benhadad king of Syria; the name signifies pleasantness.

He was a mighty man of valour, but a leper.

A little captive maid of Israel told her mistress of the prophet in Samaria.

Being sent to Elisha, he was bidden to wash seven times in Jordan, and his flesh came again as the flesh of a little child.

He confessed the God of Israel, and took with him two mules' burden of earth to build an altar.

Key Scripture

2Ki 5:1 — "Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper."

2Ki 5:14 — "Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean."

2Ki 5:15 — "And he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him: and he said, Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel: now therefore, I pray thee, take a blessing of thy servant."

Luk 4:27 — "And many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian."

Modern Corruption

Naaman is preached as a lesson in humility and obedience, which he is; what the Lord Jesus made of him is sovereign election running past the covenant people to a foreign soldier.

expand to see more

Everyone preaches Naaman's pride, and rightly — the great man rehearsing in advance how the prophet ought to come out and wave his hand is one of the most recognisable portraits in Scripture. But the use the Lord Jesus made of the story in the synagogue at Nazareth was different and far more offensive. He said that there were many lepers in Israel in Elisha's day and not one of them was cleansed — only the Syrian. Israelite lepers by the score, a prophet in the land, and the healing went to a Gentile officer of the army that raided Israel's borders. His hearers, Luke says, were filled with wrath and led Him to the brow of the hill to cast Him down headlong. Sovereign, discriminating mercy is not a doctrine invented by Calvin; it is the doctrine that nearly got the Lord killed before His ministry was a month old.

The other thing usually mishandled is Naaman's last request. He asks pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon when he supports his master's arm, and Elisha answers, “Go in peace.” Some read this as licence for the believer to conform outwardly in an idolatrous setting; it will not carry that weight, and the three young men before Nebuchadnezzar's image settle the matter for a case of actual worship. What the exchange does show is a new convert with a real conscience about a real difficulty, and a prophet who did not load him with a rule he had not been given. Elisha neither approved the bowing nor pronounced on it; he blessed a man at the beginning of his obedience. Pastors would do well to notice the restraint.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Na'aman (H5283), from na'em (H5276), to be pleasant; tsara'ath (H6883), leprosy; taphal / tabal (H2881), to dip.

expand to see more

Hebrew Na'aman (H5283) — Naaman, “pleasantness”; the same root as Naomi.

Hebrew tsara'ath (H6883) — the leprosy of the law; a ceremonial uncleanness that pictured sin's defilement.

Hebrew tabal (H2881) — to dip, immerse; the verb of the seven washings in Jordan.

Hebrew Rimmon (H7417) — Rimmon, the Syrian thunder-god in whose house Naaman had to attend his master.

Greek Neeman (G3497) — Naaman; named by the Lord Jesus at Nazareth (Luk 4:27).

Usage

"“A mighty man in valour, but he was a leper” — the sentence that turns on one word."

"“His flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child” — cleansing by an ordinary washing."

"“There is no God in all the earth, but in Israel” — a Syrian's confession."
